title: What is sustainable living?
summary: Sustainability is more than just a checklist.
body_text: Google "sustainable living" and you'll find a lot of lists—sometimes fairly exhaustive lists—that offer simple steps you can take to green up your life. Replace your old incandescent light bulbs with LEDs. Drip dry your laundry. Walk to work. Etc., etc. These sorts of documents are useful, but sometimes a list makes it easy to select low-hanging fruit, rather than really pausing to think about the consequences of our lives. To live sustainably—to build a life that does not overly drain the world's resources—requires a deeper understanding of the concept. Which is what I'll try to provide here. 📚 Jump to section: What is sustainability? Where does this idea come from? What can I do to live sustainably? What is sustainability? As the word implies, sustainability is the practice of sustaining the world. Our lives depend on resources that come from the earth: food grown in the soil; wood pulled from forests; fuels extracted from deep underground. Sustainability involves using these resources at rates that allow for their replacement or replenishment. Sustainability is like "net zero," but for more than just carbon. It involves living at a pace that allows Earth's resources to be replenished. "Net zero" has become a familiar phrase these days, an update on the idea of being " carbon neutral "—ensuring that you are offsetting your carbon emissions. You can think of sustainable living as being net zero not just in terms of carbon emissions, but in terms of resource consumption more broadly. Image credit: Doughnut Economics / Creative Commons Scientists have identified nine "planetary boundaries," hypothetical red lines that, once crossed, might mean irrecoverable damage. Among other categories, there are boundaries for how much freshwater we're withdrawing, how much CO2 we're releasing, and how quickly species are disappearing. (For a full accounting of the planetary boundaries, see this post .) A fully sustainable life needs to consider all of these categories—and even more. Human culture and society deserves to be sustained too. Consider the United Nations concept of "sustainable tourism": it targets ecosystems and social systems both. Does everyone have access to good, fair jobs? Are traditional cultures being preserved? The economist Kate Raworth has added some of these considerations to the planetary boundaries to create a doughnut-shaped ideal zone: she proposes using few enough resources to ensure we don't cross any red lines, but notes that we need to use enough resources—and distribute them fairly—so as to provide the necessities to everyone. Where does this idea come from? Many cultures—particularly indigenous cultures—were built around economic and spiritual practices that emphasized sustainability. (That's why one of the best forest-protection strategies is to protect Indigenous-held lands .) In European cultures, though, sustainability began to emerge as a definable concept by the seventeenth century, when a scientific approach to forestry emerged. Foresters hoped to be able to continuously harvest timber. This idea of "wise use" of natural resources spread widely in the late nineteenth century. As I've covered previously , though, there were often debates about what wise use of nature really meant. Some indigenous cultures have emphasized sustainability for millennia; in Western cultures, ecology itself was not a well-understood concept until into the twentieth century. In the mid-twentieth century, new thinkers like Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson brought an understanding of ecology to a wider audience, and in 1972 an influential report called The Limits to Growth used computer models to suggest our economy could not continue at the same pace without tarnishing the earth. By the 1980s, the idea of "sustainable development" had become common phrase at organizations like the UN. So what can I do to live sustainably? With that context in place, we can now turn to more concrete actions. Let's start with climate, since that's our major focus here at Wren. I've written previously about practical steps you can take as an individual to reduce your carbon impact, and I encourage you to read that post entirely. But here are some overarching considerations. Where does your energy come from? The writer David Roberts has advised readers to " electrify everything ": your car, your stove, everything you own. For now, your electrical devices may still run on fossil fuels, since that's where much of our electricity comes from. Still, a centralized power plant is more efficient than many separate gas-burning engines. And since over time our electrical grid is likely to turn to renewables, this move will pay off further long term. How do you move through the world? Transportation is a major source of carbon emissions. Can you walk or use a bike to replace you car, at least occasionally? What about public transportation? To be truly sustainable, you may need to cut back on your travel, for work and for pleasure both. It's time to love where you live. (You might also read our full post on sustainable travel .) What do you eat? Our food is made with fossil fuels—they power our tractors and the trucks that carry our food. But agriculture impacts many other aspects of the environment, too: fertilizers cause algal blooms in lakes and oceans; forests are cut down so as to clear farmland. A vegetarian diet vastly reduces on your environmental footprint—and a vegan diet even more so, since dairy has a large carbon impact. A simple first step is just cutting back on how much meat you eat. When it comes to food, though, there are more variables than just diet. The more you know about the farmers and producers you buy from, the better: what kinds of fertilizers do they use? Where is the farm located? Buying local only has a minor environmental impact, but it can have an important economic impact, since it keeps dollars cycling within a community. How you eat matters, too. If compost your food scraps rather than trash them, you can help reduce the need for fertilizers and helps hold greenhouse gases in the soils. If you don't garden yourself, see if your town has a composting program. Or start a garden! Growing your own food is one more step closer to true sustainability. How much stuff do you use? People sometimes talk about the "three Rs" —reduce, reuse, recycle. These are good steps, but it's worth adding one more : refuse. Refuse to buy anything you don't really need. Pollution, especially plastic pollution, is a pressing problem; and since today's plastic is produced from petroleum, anything you buy that contains plastic—which is almost everything these days—adds a bit more emissions to the world. What are your friends doing? One final note: Our modern world, from our electrical grid to our food system, is not built with sustainability in mind. To try to become truly net zero can make for a rather difficult life . Certainly your life choices can wind up becoming an important example for others—but ultimately the world needs a major overhaul. You might consider joining organizations like the Sunrise Movement or the Citizens' Climate Lobby . Expanding your impact through advocacy is as important—or perhaps more important—than anything you might do individually. Ready to start working towards sustainability? Sign up for Climate Camp , a weekly email series that will walk you through personalized first steps.

title: Best Virtual Staging Software in 2026: 7 Tools Compared
summary: Compare the 7 best virtual staging tools of 2026 on price, speed, and features — see which wins for budget, luxury, DIY, and all-in-one listing visuals.
body_text: Best Virtual Staging Software in 2026: 7 Tools Compared Virtual staging turns an empty room into a furnished, listing-ready photo — without renting a single piece of furniture. In 2026 the market has split into three camps: ultra-fast AI tools that return an image in seconds, designer-led services that hand-edit over 24–48 hours, and all-in-one suites that cover the whole listing, not just one photo. There's no single "best" — the right tool depends on what you're optimizing for. Below we compare seven leading platforms on the criteria that actually change your results, name a winner in each category, and explain who each one is really for. Quick verdict: For a single cheap staged photo, the sub-dollar AI tools win. For a complete set of listing visuals — consistent furniture across every angle, furniture removal, 360° views, and property video from one platform — Apply Design is the best all-in-one choice. How we compared them We scored each platform on five criteria: Price per image — real cost at typical volume, not the headline teaser rate. Turnaround — how fast you get a usable image back. Output quality & realism — furniture that looks placed, not pasted. Scope of features — does it only stage one photo, or handle the full listing (multi-angle, removal, 360°, video)? Support & trust — real customer support and adoption by established brands. Pricing below reflects published rates at time of writing and shifts often — confirm current pricing on each vendor's site before deciding. At-a-glance comparison Apply Design — pay-as-you-go, ~$7–$10.50/image (coins, no subscription), ~10 min. Best for: all-in-one — staging, DIY restyling, removal, 360°, video. AI HomeDesign — monthly/yearly subscription (credit-based), seconds. Best for: high-volume subscribers. Virtual Staging AI — monthly/yearly subscription, $16–$79/mo (6–150 photos), ~10 sec. Best for: cheapest DIY subscription. RoomStaging — monthly subscription, 15–30 sec. Best for: bulk speed. BoxBrownie — pay per image, ~$24/image, 24–48 hr. Best for: human-edited, workflow bundling. Styldod — pay per image, $23/image ($16 at 8+), 24–48 hr. Best for: luxury listings. PhotoUp — monthly subscription (credits), $39–$399/mo, 24–48 hr. Best for: photographers reselling staging. Billing model matters: Apply Design, BoxBrownie, and Styldod are pay-as-you-go — you only pay for what you use. AI HomeDesign, Virtual Staging AI, RoomStaging, and PhotoUp require a monthly subscription. Category winners Best overall / all-in-one: Apply Design Cheapest single image: AI HomeDesign Fastest single image: RoomStaging / Virtual Staging AI (sub-minute) Most complete feature set (staging + restyling + removal + 360° + video): Apply Design Best human-edited: BoxBrownie Best for luxury: Styldod Best for photographers (white-label): PhotoUp 1. Apply Design — Best overall / all-in-one listing visuals Most tools on this list do one thing — stage a single photo. Apply Design is a full listing-visuals suite that covers the entire job, which is why it wins the broadest use case for working agents and photographers. Here's the complete range: Auto Staging — automatically furnishes vacant rooms in a chosen style. DIY editing — full manual control to place, swap, and adjust furniture yourself, with unlimited/endless revisions. Multiple styles on one room — restage the same room in as many different looks as you want (modern, Scandinavian, farmhouse, etc.) to compare options or match buyer demographics. Multi-angle consistency — the same furniture layout rendered correctly across every angle of a room, so a gallery looks coherent instead of showing a different sofa in every shot. Almost no fast/cheap tool handles this. Furniture removal — clear out existing furniture and clutter to reset a room. AI enhancements — automatic image cleanup and quality improvements. 360° views — immersive walkthrough-style room views. Property video — generate listing video from your images, no separate videography tool. Speed & support: ~10 minutes per image, with 24/7 live customer support — rare at this price point. Trust: used by 4,000+ customers. Pricing: pay-as-you-go — roughly $7–$10.50 per image depending on coin volume, with no monthly subscription required. Not the cheapest per single photo — but the only option here that delivers a complete, consistent set of listing visuals without stitching three or four separate tools together, and you only pay for what you use. Best for: agents, brokerages, and photographers who need a full listing's worth of visuals — everything from Auto Staging to DIY restyling to video — in one platform, not just one staged bedroom. 2. AI HomeDesign — Cheapest per image Genuinely the budget leader: staged, MLS-ready photos from ~$0.24 each in under five seconds, with a free tier to try. Style range is narrower (around 8), and it's single-photo staging rather than a full suite, but for sheer cost-per-image at volume it's hard to beat. Best for: high-volume agents who need many cheap single photos fast. 3. Virtual Staging AI — Cheapest DIY subscription Subscription model (from ~$16/mo, ~$1/image) with ~10-second turnaround. A low-cost way to restage rooms if per-image price is your only concern. (Note: multi-style restaging isn't unique here — Apply Design does it too, alongside removal, 360°, and video.) Best for: budget DIY users focused purely on cost per image. 4. RoomStaging — Best for bulk speed Results in 15–30 seconds and effective cost dropping to ~$0.07/photo on higher plans. Built for throughput. Best for: teams staging in bulk where per-image speed and cost dominate. 5. BoxBrownie — Best human-edited option An established photo-editing brand: real human editors, 24–48 hour turnaround, ~$24/image. Also covers image enhancement, floor plans, and day-to-dusk edits, so it's handy if you already buy photo services there. Best for: agents who want human QA and workflow consolidation. 6. Styldod — Best for luxury listings Designer-led realism aimed at high-end properties where photo quality directly moves list price. Best for: luxury and spec-grade listings. 7. PhotoUp — Best for photographers reselling staging A white-label workflow built for studio operators who resell staging to their own clients under their own brand. Best for: real estate photographers running a studio. How to choose You only care about the lowest possible price per image → AI HomeDesign or Virtual Staging AI. You want a human editor to guarantee the result → BoxBrownie or Styldod. You're a photographer reselling under your brand → PhotoUp. You want to do it all — Auto Staging and hands-on DIY restyling, test multiple styles on one room, keep furniture consistent across angles, remove furniture, add 360° and video → Apply Design. The cheap tools win a single image. The whole listing is a different job — and that's where an all-in-one suite pays for itself. Why virtual staging matters Staged listings attract more clicks and can sell faster than empty-room photos, at a fraction of the cost of physical staging. But buyers scroll fast — an inconsistent gallery (different furniture in every shot, one bare room, no video) undercuts the effect. A complete, coherent set of visuals is what actually holds attention. FAQ How much does virtual staging cost in 2026? Anywhere from ~$0.24 per image on budget AI tools to ~$24+ per image for human-edited services. All-in-one suites like Apply Design run roughly $7–$10.50 per image but include multi-angle staging, furniture removal, 360°, and video. What's the fastest virtual staging software? The fastest single-image tools (RoomStaging, Virtual Staging AI) return an image in under a minute. Apply Design takes ~10 minutes per image but produces a full, angle-consistent visual set rather than one standalone photo. Is AI virtual staging good enough for MLS listings? Yes. For standard living rooms, bedrooms, kitchens, and dining rooms — the bulk of what agents stage — modern AI output is MLS-ready and hard to distinguish from physically staged rooms. What's the difference between AI staging tools and an all-in-one suite? Most AI tools stage a single photo. A suite like Apply Design also does furniture removal, multi-angle consistency, 360° views, and property video — the full set of assets a listing needs. Which virtual staging software is best overall? For a single cheap photo, budget AI tools win. For a complete listing's worth of consistent visuals, Apply Design is the strongest all-in-one option.

title: Newsweek Names Bank of Hawai‘i One of “America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026”
summary: Newsweek Names Bank of Hawai‘i One of “America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026”
body_text: Newsroom Newsweek Names Bank of Hawai‘i One of “America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026” Of 1,000 companies nationwide, Bank of Hawai‘i is the only Hawai‘i-based company on the list HONOLULU July 17th, 2026 Bank of Hawai‘i is named on a national ranking of “America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026” by Newsweek . A total of 1,000 U.S. companies are listed. Bank of Hawai‘i is one of 24 banks nationwide to be recognized and the only company in the state of Hawai‘i to receive the accolade. The ranking was published by Newsweek on July 16 and can be found here . “We are humbled to be the only company in Hawai‘i named to Newsweek’s list. It speaks to a culture that puts people first and is especially meaningful because it reflects the voices of our own teammates. It affirms that the family-friendly benefits we’ve built are truly making a difference in the lives of our employees, and we remain committed to fostering a supportive workplace where parents and families can thrive,” said Sharlene Ginoza-Lee, chief people officer at Bank of Hawai‘i. Bank of Hawai‘i continues to provide a variety of family-friendly benefits/programs, such as its paid parental leave and the Bank of Hawai‘i Foundation Scholarship. Bank of Hawai‘i’s paid parental leave provides 4-6 weeks of paid time off, depending on years of service. Employees may use the time during the first 12 months of welcoming a new baby, adoption or foster care placement; and for added flexibility, the time does not need to be used all at once. Now in its 12th year, the Bank of Hawai‘i Foundation Scholarship offers financial assistance to college-bound children and grandchildren of bank employees. Since the program’s inception in January 2014, Bank of Hawai‘i Foundation has awarded 317 scholarships totaling $1,106,000 through its program administrator Hawai‘i Community Foundation. Newsweek partnered with Plant-A Insights Group, a market research firm, to compile its fourth list of “America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026.” The comprehensive study combines a large-scale national survey, extensive desk research, and third-party data to identify organizations with more than 1,000 employees that provide exceptional workplaces for parents. The national survey was conducted between April 2025 and October 2025, gathering company reviews from more than 100,000 working parents, which provided insights and metrics including backup childcare, paid family leave policies exceeding federal minimums, adoption assistance programs, employer-contributed flexible spending accounts, and subsidized cryopreservation benefits. Additionally, results from three previous studies conducted between 2022 and 2024 have been incorporated into the overall findings with a reduced weight. In total, more than 300,000 working parents were surveyed between 2022 and 2025, making America’s Greatest Workplaces for Parents & Families 2026 one of the nation’s largest independent employee studies focused on working families. title: Why High-Performing Teams Start with Trust
summary: When people understand where different perspectives come from, disagreement becomes more productive.
body_text: Organizations often focus on strategy, technology and execution when pursuing growth. But behind every successful strategy is something less visible: a team that trusts one another enough to challenge ideas and solve problems together, moving forward with confidence. That lesson has become increasingly clear through the Advanced Surgery Leadership Team’s ongoing Cohesive Teams journey. Over the past several years, team members have participated in facilitated sessions designed to strengthen trust and improve communication, creating greater alignment. What started as a leadership development exercise evolved into a practical framework for how the team collaborates every day. The experience helped employees better understand how teammates think, communicate and make decisions. Through assessments, team discussions and structured exercises, participants gained insight into individual strengths as well as personality styles and motivations. The result was not greater agreement. It was greater understanding. When people understand where different perspectives come from, disagreement becomes more productive. Teams become more comfortable discussing difficult topics and challenging assumptions, working through conflict constructively. That shift has had a measurable impact on collaboration within the team. Meeting structures became more intentional. Communication improved. Decision-making accelerated because employees developed greater trust in one another’s intentions and expertise. For global teams , these benefits become even more important. When employees work across different sites, countries and functions, relationship-building cannot be left to chance. Regular check-ins and opportunities for personal connection help create the trust needed to collaborate effectively. The team’s experience reinforces a broader principle relevant to organizations of all sizes: Trust is not a soft skill. It is a business capability. Trust enables faster decisions. It improves collaboration. It creates space for healthy conflict and stronger innovation. It helps teams remain resilient through change. As organizations grow and become more interconnected, investing in team cohesion becomes increasingly important. The strongest teams are not the ones that avoid disagreement. They are the ones that build enough trust to navigate disagreement well. For the Advanced Surgery Leadership Team, that investment continues today. Their experience demonstrates that cohesive leadership is not a destination. It is an ongoing practice that helps teams perform at their best while creating stronger outcomes for the business. As we continue growing as One Novanta, those lessons become increasingly valuable.
